---
order: 6
unit: detail
title: Verbs that do the work
summary: "A precise verb can say what a verb and an adverb need two words for (ran very fast becomes sprinted). The tense tells the reader when something happens: past, present or future. And an adverb group adds how, where, when or how much (very quietly, just outside, quite recently). A writer picks all three to say exactly what is meant."
language: maths
node: [AC9E6LA06 n1, AC9E6LA06 n2, AC9E6LA06 n3]
explainPicture: { ref: text.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Dived does the work of jumped very quickly. A precise verb says in one word what a plain verb and an adverb need two for." }
hook: "'Drank very quickly' or 'gulped'. Which one is the writer's best choice, and why?"
---
Three tools make a sentence more exact.

- **A precise verb:** *gulped* says what *drank very quickly* needs three words for.
- **The tense:** *scored* (past), *scores* (present) or *will score* (future) tells the reader when.
- **An adverb group:** *very quietly* (how), *just outside* (where), *quite recently* (when) or *very much* (how much) adds detail to a verb.

## Predict: one word instead of three

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Predicting the single verb for a wordy phrase shows students that a precise verb carries the meaning of the extra words."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "'Mia said very quietly that she was nervous.' Which single verb could replace 'said very quietly'?"
  options: ["whispered", "shouted", "argued", "asked"]
  actual: "whispered. It means 'said very quietly', so the sentence needs no extra words."
```

## Try: choose the sharper verb

```step
stage: run
insight: "Choosing the verb that matches each wordy phrase shows a precise verb does the work of a plain verb and an adverb."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#run", height: 460 }
hint: ["Read the wordy sentence, then choose the one verb that means the same.", "Test each choice: does it mean the same as the wordy phrase?"]
smaller:
  check: { type: question, q: "Which single verb means 'drank very quickly'?", options: ["gulped", "sipped", "tasted"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "Sipped is a slow, small drink.", "Tasted is a small try, not a quick drink."], explain: "Gulped means to drink very quickly, so it replaces drank very quickly." }
check: { type: board, text: "Choose the single verb that means the same as each wordy phrase.", when: "n_gaps_right = 3", explain: "Crept means walked very quietly, studied means looked at very carefully, and devoured means ate very quickly. Each one replaces a plain verb and an adverb." }
```

Were you right about Mia? Whispered meant 'said very quietly'.

## Worked example: verbs, tense and adverbs

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Matching phrases to precise verbs, catching a plain verb with an adverb, and choosing the tense a report needs shows each word choice is made for a reason."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: match
      q: "Match each wordy phrase to the one verb that says it."
      pairs:
        - ["walked with heavy, angry steps", "stomped"]
        - ["looked angrily at", "glared at"]
        - ["laughed in a silly, quiet way", "giggled"]
        - ["picked up quickly and firmly", "grabbed"]
      explain: "Each precise verb carries both the action and how it was done, so the sentence needs no adverb."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Here is Nib's match report, one sentence per line. One line uses a plain verb and an adverb where one precise verb would be sharper. Click it."
      answer: 2
      fault: logic
      misconception: weak-verb
      explain: "Line 2: 'ran very fast' could be 'sprinted' or 'raced'. One precise verb says what the plain verb and the adverb did together."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A report posted the day after a match tells what happened. Which tense does it mostly use?"
      options: ["Past: scored, kicked, won", "Future: will score, will kick", "Present: scores, kicks", "No tense at all"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Future tense looks ahead to events that have not happened.", "Present tense would make the match sound as if it is happening now.", "Every verb has a tense."]
      explain: "The match is over, so the report mostly says what happened: scored, kicked, won."
```

### Three ways to sharpen a sentence

```worked
\text{Look at the verb} :: Is there one verb that says what the verb and the adverb say together?
\text{Check the tense} :: When does this happen: past, present or future?
\text{Add an adverb group only if it helps} :: How, where, when or how much? Does the reader need it?
```

Now match the phrases to verbs.

## Vary: choose the tense

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Choosing the verb form that fits each time clue shows the tense is set by when the event happens."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#vary", height: 320 }
hint: ["Look for a word in each sentence that says when.", "Past tense for what already happened, present for what is true now, will plus a verb for what is coming."]
check: { type: board, text: "Choose the verb form that fits each time clue.", when: "n_gaps_right = 3", explain: "Yesterday points to the past (visited), these days points to the present (leaves), and next week points to the future (will plant)." }
```

## Practise: adverb groups

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Colouring adverb groups by what they add shows they are not all about how."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#practise", height: 330 }
hint: ["Chain 1 is how (manner), Chain 2 is when (time), Chain 3 is where (place).", "Click the whole adverb group, such as 'really slowly', not just one word."]
check: { type: board, text: "Colour the adverb groups: how (Chain 1), when (Chain 2) and where (Chain 3).", when: "chains_ok = 3 and n_stray = 0", explain: "Quite softly and extremely carefully say how. Very early says when. Just outside says where." }
```

## Make: a match report

In your own document, write a match report of at least five sentences (at least 50 words) about a match or game you know, or one you make up. Tell what happened in the order it happened. Use at least two precise verbs and two adverb groups. Keep to the past tense.

Here is one example: "Our team played Hillside on Saturday morning. The striker **sprinted** down the wing and **crossed** the ball. Hillside's keeper **dived** but missed it. The crowd roared as the ball hit the net. Our captain lifted the trophy, and everyone cheered **very loudly**."

Then swap with a partner. Underline each precise verb and each adverb group in each other's report. Is every verb in the past tense? Does each adverb group help?

```step
stage: make
insight: "Writing five sentences of a match report uses precise verbs, past tense and adverb groups where they help a reader see the match."
hint: ["Choose a match or a game you know (or make one up). Write what happened, in the order it happened.", "Use at least two precise verbs and two adverb groups. Keep to the past tense."]
check: { type: reflect, text: "I wrote a match report of at least five sentences with precise verbs, adverb groups and the past tense, and a partner and I underlined them and checked each one." }
```

## In your own writing

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "Checking a real piece of writing for plain verbs with adverbs puts the move to use outside the board."
check: { type: reflect, text: "I read a piece of my own writing and replaced at least one plain verb and adverb with a single precise verb." }
```

```teacher
summary: Students learn that precise verbs, the right tense and adverb groups
  make a sentence more exact. They choose a one-word verb for a wordy phrase,
  match phrases to verbs, catch a plain verb with an adverb, choose the tense a
  report needs, choose verb forms from time clues, colour adverb groups by what
  they add and write a match report in their own document.
time: 50
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 6 min · Practise 6
  min · Make (in their own document) and own writing 18 min
goals:
  - I can replace a plain verb and an adverb with one precise verb.
  - I can choose past, present or future for what I am telling.
  - "I can say what an adverb group adds: how, where, when or how much."
  - I can write a match report that uses all three well.
struggle: Students pile on adverbs ('ran very, very quickly') or swap in a long
  word that is not exact. Ask 'does this verb say more than the plain one?' and
  let them check against what they meant.
before: >
  Do the Try board yourself: three wordy sentences, three precise verbs.


  The one idea: choose the verb, the tense and the adverb group on purpose. This
  lesson covers AC9E6LA06 nodes 1 to 3 (precise verb selection, elaborated
  tenses, adverb groups for precision).


  ACARA's **elaborated tenses** here means the different ways English refers to
  time: simple present, simple past and future time expressions (will plus a
  verb). The lesson keeps to those. It does not teach perfect or continuous
  tenses; 'was planting' appears only as a wrong choice.


  A precise verb is not always a longer one. 'Said' is often the best verb; the
  aim is exact, not fancy. The board plants verbs whose meanings are clear from
  the wordy phrase.


  An **adverb group** is an adverb with a word that modifies it (very quietly,
  just outside). The lesson sticks to these; prepositional phrases (along the
  creek) are covered in other lessons.


  The facts and sentences are made up for the lesson.
running:
  - "Predict: ask which word 'whispered' replaced, and what the sentence lost."
  - "Try: after choosing, ask when the plain verb and an adverb would be the
    better choice."
  - "Worked example: Nib's report. Ask which single verb would say 'ran very
    fast'."
  - "Vary: ask what time clue pointed to each tense."
  - "Make: students write in their own document, then partners underline each
    precise verb and adverb group, and check the tense."
stuck:
  - see: A student chooses 'stomped' for 'walked very quietly'.
    ask: Does this verb mean the same as the wordy phrase?
    fix: Match meaning first. Test by saying the wordy phrase and the single verb
      side by side.
  - see: A student's report switches between 'scored' and 'scores'.
    ask: Has this match already happened?
    fix: Choose one tense for the whole report and check every verb.
  - see: A student colours 'along the creek' as an adverb group.
    ask: Is it an adverb with a modifier, or a phrase that starts with a
      preposition?
    fix: "An adverb group is an adverb and its modifier: very early, just outside."
stretch: Take a paragraph from a class novel and find one plain verb with an
  adverb. Rewrite it with one precise verb. Did the author make a better choice,
  or did your version?
support: "A verb ladder: ran, hurried, raced, dashed, sprinted, from plain to precise."
leads: >
  Next in Building sentences: compound-complex sentences, which combine what you
  know about clauses.


  Tense reappears in Shaping sentences, where students keep it steady across a
  whole passage.
exit:
  q: "'The kettle boiled very loudly.' Replace 'boiled very loudly' with one
    precise verb, or explain why the sentence is fine."
  a: Roared or bubbled fits, though 'boiled' alone is also fine if the loudness
    does not matter. The point is to choose on purpose.
explain: >
  Three tools make a sentence more exact.


  - **A precise verb:** *gulped* says what *drank very quickly* needs three
  words for.

  - **The tense:** *scored* (past), *scores* (present), *will score* (future).

  - **An adverb group:** *very quietly* (how), *just outside* (where), *quite
  recently* (when).


  Pick the verb that says exactly what happened, keep the tense that matches the
  time, and add an adverb group only when it helps.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Is a longer verb always a better verb?
    prompts:
      - Read 'She said she was fine' and 'She insisted she was fine'. Which is
        more exact? Which is better?
      - When is plain 'said' the best choice?
    notes: A precise verb is one that fits the meaning. Plain 'said' is often right,
      especially in dialogue where the words carry the feeling. The aim is to
      choose on purpose, not to find a bigger word.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Mime the verb
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Write 'walked' on the board. Students mime it. Then call out 'tiptoed',
        'stomped' and 'trudged' for the class to mime. Ask what each shows that
        'walked' does not.
      notes: The difference between the miming shows what a precise verb adds.
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: Underline and check
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Partners underline the precise verbs and adverb groups in each other's
        reports. They check every verb is in the past tense.
      notes: If a report switches tense, mark where and ask which tense they meant.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Which one verb?
      type: question
      q: Which single verb means 'spoke in a very loud voice'?
      options:
        - shouted
        - whispered
        - mumbled
      answer: 0
      explain: Shouted means to speak very loudly. Whispered is quiet and mumbled is
        unclear.
```

# groups by what they add).

# region: run
widget: cohesion
p: Wordy: The cat walked very quietly across the roof. Sharper: The cat [[{crept|stomped|sprinted}=crept]] across the roof.
p: Wordy: He looked at the map very carefully. Sharper: He [[{glanced at|studied|ignored}=studied]] the map.
p: Wordy: Ben ate his lunch very quickly. Sharper: Ben [[{devoured|nibbled|sipped}=devoured]] his lunch.
# endregion

# region: vary
widget: cohesion
p: Yesterday our class [[{visits|visited|will visit}=visited]] the farm. These days the bus [[{left|leaves|will leave}=leaves]] at eight each morning. Next week our class [[{planted|will plant|was planting}=will plant]] a garden.
# endregion

# region: practise
widget: cohesion
mode: chain
colours: 3
p: We arrived [[very early#b]] and waited [[just outside#c]]. The ranger spoke [[quite softly#a]] and checked the gate [[extremely carefully#a]].
# endregion

widget: cohesion
answer: on
p: Wordy: The goalkeeper jumped very quickly to her left. Sharper: The goalkeeper [[{dived|walked|waited}=dived]] to her left.
